mcqs.question: Why does an object detector's training loss combine a regression term and a classification term, rather than using a single classification loss like a standard image classifier?
options: Detection has no localization component, so the regression term is unnecessary and vestigial
Classification loss alone is always sufficient because bounding boxes can be inferred afterward from the class label
The regression term exists only to speed up training convergence, not to affect accuracy

Detection requires solving two distinct sub-problems simultaneously — where the object is (box coordinates, a regression problem) and what it is (class label, a classification problem) — so the loss must supervise both
mcqs.explanation: Detection is fundamentally a dual task: getting the box coordinates right is a regression problem (continuous values), while getting the label right is a classification problem, and both must be jointly supervised for the model to learn either correctly. The regression term is essential, not vestigial (A is false), it directly determines localization accuracy, not just convergence speed (C is false), and box coordinates cannot be inferred from a class label alone (D is false).

mcqs.question: Why do most detectors predict small coordinate offsets relative to predefined anchor boxes, rather than predicting raw box coordinates from scratch?
options: Predicting offsets from a reasonable starting guess (the anchor) is an easier learning problem than predicting absolute coordinates with no prior, since the anchor already approximates plausible object shapes and locations
Raw coordinate prediction is mathematically impossible for neural networks
Anchor boxes are only used to speed up inference, with no effect on training difficulty
Anchors eliminate the need for a classification head entirely
mcqs.explanation: Anchors give the model a strong prior — plausible sizes and aspect ratios at every location — so the network only needs to learn small corrective offsets rather than solving an unconstrained coordinate-regression problem from nothing, which is a meaningfully easier optimization target. Raw coordinate regression is not impossible, just harder to train well (B is false), anchors affect training difficulty directly, not just inference speed (C is false), and detectors still need a classification head regardless of anchor use (D is false).

mcqs.question: What is the core architectural trade-off two-stage detectors like Faster R-CNN make by separating region proposal from classification?
options: They gain speed at some cost to accuracy, the opposite trade-off from one-stage detectors

They spend extra compute running two sequential networks (proposal, then per-region classification), generally trading speed for the accuracy benefit of letting the classifier focus only on plausible regions
The two stages run fully in parallel, so there is no speed cost at all
Region proposals eliminate the need for a classification stage entirely
mcqs.explanation: Two-stage detectors run a proposal network first and then a separate classification/refinement pass on each proposed region — this sequential extra pass costs speed but lets the second stage concentrate its capacity on likely object regions rather than scanning the whole image uniformly, generally improving accuracy. This is the opposite of option A's framing (two-stage typically trades speed for accuracy, not the reverse), the stages run sequentially, not in parallel (C is false), and a classification stage is still required after proposals (D is false).

mcqs.question: Why is YOLO ("You Only Look Once") named the way it is, and what does that imply about its architecture?
options: It refers to running the model only once per video, not once per frame
It reflects that a single network pass over the whole image directly predicts all boxes and classes at once, with no separate cropping-and-reclassifying stage, unlike two-stage detectors
It means the model only detects one object per image regardless of how many are present
It refers to only using one anchor box per grid cell
mcqs.explanation: The name describes the one-stage design: the network looks at the image exactly once and simultaneously predicts class and box for every anchor location, with no separate region-proposal-then-classify pass as in two-stage detectors. It's not about video frame rate (A), YOLO detects multiple objects per image (C is false), and YOLO variants typically use multiple anchors per grid cell, not just one (D is false).

mcqs.question: An autonomous vehicle's perception system must process camera frames at 30+ fps to react in real time. Which detector family is the more natural fit, and why?
options: Two-stage detectors, because they are always more accurate under every condition
Detector family choice has no effect on achievable frame rate
One-stage detectors, because their single-pass architecture is substantially faster, meeting the hard real-time latency constraint even at some historical accuracy cost versus two-stage detectors
Neither family can run at 30 fps on any hardware
mcqs.explanation: Real-time constraints like this are exactly what one-stage detectors (YOLO/SSD) are designed for — their single-pass architecture achieves the frame rates two-stage detectors typically cannot reach, making them the standard choice for latency-critical applications like autonomous driving despite some historical accuracy trade-off. Two-stage detectors are not universally more accurate under every condition (A overclaims), detector architecture directly determines achievable throughput (C is false), and modern one-stage detectors on suitable hardware do achieve real-time frame rates (D is false).

mcqs.question: A detector outputs five overlapping boxes around a single dog, all with high confidence. What removes the duplicates before final output, and how does it decide which box to keep?
options: mAP calculation silently averages duplicate boxes into one before reporting
The softmax function automatically merges overlapping boxes
Anchor boxes are removed after training, eliminating duplicates automatically
Non-Max Suppression — it keeps the highest-confidence box and discards other boxes overlapping it above an IoU threshold, repeating for remaining boxes
mcqs.explanation: NMS is the standard post-processing step for exactly this problem: it sorts predictions by confidence, keeps the top one, suppresses other predictions that overlap it above an IoU threshold (commonly 0.5), and repeats for the remaining boxes until none are left — turning a cluster of near-duplicates into one final prediction. Softmax operates on class scores, not spatial overlap (B is false), anchors are a training-time construct unrelated to inference-time duplicate removal (C is false), and mAP is an evaluation metric computed after final predictions, not a de-duplication step (D is false).

mcqs.question: Two boxes have an IoU of 0.05 against each other. What does this value indicate, and where would it matter in a detection pipeline?
options: The boxes barely overlap at all; in evaluation this would typically mean the prediction does not count as a correct localization against that ground-truth box (below the usual 0.5 threshold)
The boxes overlap almost completely; this would trigger NMS to suppress one of them
IoU only applies during training, never during evaluation or NMS
An IoU of 0.05 is not a valid value and indicates a computation error
mcqs.explanation: IoU close to 0 means the predicted box and ground truth (or two predictions) have very little spatial overlap — well below the standard 0.5 threshold used both in NMS (to decide if two predictions are "the same" detection) and in evaluation (to decide if a prediction counts as correctly localizing an object). It would not trigger NMS suppression, since NMS suppresses highly overlapping boxes, the opposite case (A is false), IoU is used in both NMS and evaluation, not exclusively training (C is false), and 0.05 is a perfectly valid, just low, IoU value (D is false).

mcqs.question: Why does mAP use the area under a per-class precision-recall curve instead of a single accuracy number, when scoring a detector?
options: Because accuracy is undefined for any multi-class task

Because detection involves ranking predictions by confidence across a range of thresholds, and area-under-curve captures performance across that whole range, including the trade-off between false positives and false negatives, which a single accuracy score cannot represent
Because precision-recall curves are easier to compute than accuracy
Because mAP is only used for single-class detection problems
mcqs.explanation: Detection involves a confidence threshold choice that trades off precision against recall, and a single accuracy number would hide that trade-off and be sensitive to an arbitrary threshold pick; Average Precision integrates over the whole precision-recall curve, capturing performance across all thresholds and across both false positives and false negatives, then mAP averages this across classes. Accuracy is well-defined for multi-class tasks generally, just poorly suited here (B is false), computational ease isn't the reason (C), and mAP is explicitly designed to handle and average across multiple classes (D is false).
